doc.title: Rick Margitza interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 22, 2024

title: Demonstrating the technique on saxophone
summary: He plays examples of moving minor triads by major thirds and half steps, practised across the whole range.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Okay. The actual pitch of the C sharp, in other words if you’re playing at the high end of your sax or in the middle, is that part of your decision to play it? Where it’s actually coming out in relationship to the piano chords or —

No, not really. Maybe because of where I was before in terms of the line, but not in relationship to like the range of the piano. But I don’t know what this is going to sound like but just so quickly now if you’re thinking A minor [plays chord on sax] Right? So when I hear that and am thinking about the three minor chords that are related by major thirds. So you have [plays saxophone]. So if we’re hearing something with this as the root [plays one note] we get that in our ears, if the bass is playing it or the piano or whatever, you can go [plays]. So there I started immediately at a C sharp minor, went up to F minor, back to C sharp and then back to A. So it depends if you have sixteen measures of A minor or you have two measures, about how much time you have to get to where you want to go. [Plays]
Is that technique under your fingers now?

It’s also like I said, it’s a combination of it being between in my fingers and in my ears. And hearing that it’s not anything that all of a sudden like afraid of playing — that’s kind of one of the first notes I’ll go for sometimes. And a good way to practice that is to just play an A minor on the piano and play that wrong note and listen to where it wants to go. Right? So I don’t have a keyboard here with me but if we’re going [plays sax] we’re getting that in our ears, and somebody goes [plays one note]. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

You know it just occurred to me it’s almost the opposite of — if you’re playing an A blues there’s a C sharp in the chord but the C natural is like the blue note, which you’d go to that constantly. And so you’re kind of flipping harmonically — you’ve got the major against the minor.

As opposed to the minor against the major. Yeah. That’s part of it. Except see when I’m playing the blues and we play the blue note I’m not really thinking that, well sometimes I am but I’m normally not thinking about that as a group of triads in relationship to A, but just the note that wants to go up a half step.

And the same thing even when you’re playing C sharp over A minor you can just think about it as [plays] so that’s just going up the A minor triad [plays] but at that point I’m not playing a C sharp minor triad or anything it’s just where that C sharp wants to come back down to the minor third.

But you could extend it [plays]. So that C sharp represents C sharp minor. But it also could just represent a note that wants to go a half step down to the minor third. So as a result of practicing really simple things but in all those different relationships, so minor triads and half steps [plays]. I’m only just doing a little portion of it but so that’s minor triad kind of going up and down in half steps, then whole steps [plays]. And minor triads and minor thirds [plays]. And then minor triads and major thirds [plays].
When you practice that kind of thing do you start in different places on your horn?
Yeah. I do it always from the bottom note, the lowest note possible, up to as high as I can play. So I try to cover the whole range.

So depending on — and that’s a minor triad in root position, right? So then you do the same thing with a minor triad in second inversion. Right? So that’s a completely different shape. And then when you take that through the routine it has different ramifications.
